text: Text as an array of chars ending in \0, and walking through characters.

A character array char a[105] stores text one character per box, followed by an invisible end marker '\0' . C++ can read and print it with cin and cout ; you walk it until you meet the end marker. In C++ programs a string (6.2) is usually easier, but char arrays appear in many older solutions and in grids.
hello
olleh Hello
Reading a whole line into a char array: cin.getline(a, 105) . Size the array one larger than the longest text, for the end marker.
Writing past the end of the array, or forgetting the '\0' when you build text yourself, makes cout << a print garbage after the text.
Visit each character: test it, change it, count it.

HELLO, WORLD 42 hello, world 42 Test or change Code uppercase letter? 'A' <= ch && ch <= 'Z' lowercase letter? 'a' <= ch && ch <= 'z'
to uppercase (if lowercase) ch = ch - 'a' + 'A' to lowercase (if uppercase) ch = ch - 'A' + 'a'
Letters and digits have consecutive codes, so each test is one range comparison. Writing to s[i] changes the string itself; int(s.size()) turns the unsigned length into an int for the loop.

After cin >> x , the rest of that line (often just the newline) is still waiting. The next getline returns it, so you see an empty or partial line. Fix: call one extra getline to throw it away.

The loop for (p = find(w); p != npos; p = find(w, p + 1)) visits every match, including overlapping ones. Use p + w.size() instead when matches must not overlap (P1308).
Counting a fixed short pattern such as "VK" is a simple index loop: s[i] == 'V' && s[i+1] == 'K' , with i + 1 < n (P3741).

text: Working on the digits as a string avoids overflow and keeps leading zeros under your control. Decimals, fractions and percents are split at '.' , '/' or '%' and each part handled the same way (P1553).

Parsing means walking the text and deciding by what you see. When every statement has the same shape, jump by its length (i += 5 for x:=y; ). Otherwise read token by token, or let stringstream split numbers and symbols for you (P1597, P1957).
Pictures row by row, and the right order for strings.

A vertical chart is printed top-down: row h shows a * for every column whose count is at least h. Build each row as a string and trim trailing spaces before printing (P1598).

sort on strings uses dictionary order. To glue strings into the smallest result, compare the two possible joins: put x first when x + y < y + x . The [](…) {…} is a small inline comparison function (a lambda); functions come in 入门 6 (P1603).
Files with fstream, and redirection on the command line.

By default a program reads the keyboard and prints to the screen. Contests and testing often use files instead: either the program opens the files itself, or the command line redirects the keyboard and screen to files without changing the code.

sum = 60 could not open Task C++ (fstream) read from a file ifstream in("a.in"); in >> x; write to a file ofstream out("a.out"); out << x; read a whole line getline(in, s) read until the file ends while (in >> x) check it opened if (!in) { … }
An ifstream is used exactly like cin , and an ofstream exactly like cout ; only the name changes.

a < in.txt > out.txt both

text: Redirection needs no code changes, so it is the quickest way to rerun a long sample. Keep the sample input in a file and compare outputs with fc / diff instead of by eye.

C C LANGUAGE · ADDITIONAL INFORMATION The C way, still required by some contests (for example NOIP-style rules that name the input and output files): freopen from <cstdio> reconnects stdin /stdout , and therefore cin /cout , to files. Put it at the start of main ; the rest of the program is unchanged.
Comment out freopen when testing by hand, or the program waits on a file instead of the keyboard. Luogu itself reads standard input: submit without freopen unless the problem asks for files.

Key points to memorise
1. Use string; s.size() is unsigned, so write int(s.size()) - 1.
2. (C) A C-string is a char array ending in \0; <cctype> gives isupper, isdigit, toupper, tolower.
3. cin >> s reads a word; getline(cin, s) reads a line with spaces.
4. After cin >> x, call one extra getline before reading lines.
5. while (cin >> s) and while (getline(cin, s)) read until input ends; skip \r.
6. Loop over a string with for (int i = 0; i < int(s.size()); i++); assigning to s[i] changes s.
7. Letters as numbers: ch - 'a' (0–25); tally with cnt[ch - 'a']++.
8. Caesar: (ch - 'a' + k) % 26 + 'a'; backwards add 26 before the last % 26.
9. substr(pos, len): len is a count; substr(pos) goes to the end.
10. find returns an index or string::npos; loop with find(w, p + 1).
11. Whole word, any case: lowercase both, pad with spaces, search " " + w + " ".
12. "10" < "9" is true: compare numbers as numbers.
13. to_string / stoi / stoll; long numbers stay as strings.
14. Parse by walking the text; stringstream splits numbers and symbols.
15. Pictures are printed row by row; trim trailing spaces.
16. Files: ifstream / ofstream work like cin / cout; check that the file opened.
17. Redirection: a < in.txt > out.txt, compare with fc / diff; (C) freopen does it inside the code.

2. Print s.size() - 1 for an empty string, then int(s.size()) - 1.
3. Save a sample input as in.txt and run your program with a < in.txt.
4. Write the output to out.txt and compare with the answer using fc or diff.
